newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court rules against Holocaust suspect.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court rules against Holocaust suspect.

text.p: A federal appeals court has upheld government efforts to strip the U.S. citizenship of an 80-year old man accused of participating in a massacre of Jews in Lithuania during the Second World War.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Third Circuit of Appeals, in a 2-1 decision, upheld a lower court ruling revoking the naturalised citizenship of Russian-borne Jonas Stelmokas, of Landsdowne, Pennsylvania.

His citizenship was revoked on the grounds he improperly entered the United States after concealing his service for a German-organised military unit in Lithuania that assisted in a 1941 massacre of 9,200 Jews.

"The district court correctly revoked his citizenship and ordered him to surrender his certificate of naturalisation. While many years have passed since his admission to the country and his obtaining of citizenship, it is not too late to remedy the wrong done when he was admitted," the court said in its majority opinion, which could lead to his deportation.
The ruling was handed down by the court on Tuesday and obtained by Reuters on Wednesday.

Although the appeals court's upheld the revocation of Stelmokas's citizenship, two of the three judges questioned in separate opinions the lower court's determination that Stelmokas was linked to the massacre.

Stelmokas has denied taking part in atrocities. He could not be reached for comment on the ruling and his attorney did not respond to a request for comment. The Philadelphia Inquirer quoted Stelmokas as noting the decision was not unanimous and saying he intended to pursue the case further.
"I'm going to wait to go before another panel of judges," Stelmokas told the newspaper.
Stelmokas, a retired architect, entered the country as a displaced person in 1949 and was granted citizenship in 1955.

But in 1992, the federal government's Nazi-hunting arm, the Office of Special Investigations, sued to revoke Stelmokas's citizenship, saying Stelmokas was a member of the "Schutzmannschaft," an armed unit organised by German occupiers in Lithuania that participated in persecutions of Jews and other unarmed persons.

The district court in revoking Stelmokas's citizenship last year said it concluded that he worked for at least a day as a commander of a guard unit securing a ghetto area in Kaunas, Lithuania where Jews were brutalized.
It also concluded Stelmokas's battalion took part in a massacre - the "Great Action" - of 9,200 Jews in Vilijampole, Lithuania on Oct. 28-29, and that he was on duty at the time.

In a dissent to the appeals court decision, senior circuit Judge Ruggero Aldisert said the government's case "does not rest on direct evidence, but solely on a series of rickety inferences that do not rise to the high level of proof demanded of the government." Judge Walter Stapleton said in a concurring opinion that the lower court erroneously linked him to the massacre.
